proofs.proof_tex:
The proof uses closed-relation coupling and coordinate gluing.  Define the latent compatibility class independently of the observed-law functional.  For each \(x\in\mathcal X\), let \(\mathcal Q_x\) be the set of probability laws on \(\mathcal E^4\) whose \((D(0),R(0))\)-margin is \(\mu_{0x}\), whose \((D(1),R(1))\)-margin is \(\mu_{1x}\), and which assign probability one to \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The within-arm margins obey the semicompeting-risk order by the maintained semicompeting-order assumption.  The causal identified surface set is the collection of target surfaces induced by measurable families \((Q_x:x\in\mathcal X)\) with \(Q_x\in\mathcal Q_x\) that, together with the observed treatment and censoring mechanisms, reproduce \(P\).  This class and its causal targets have been specified without using the definition of \(\Theta_I(P)\).

First, all primitives in the proposed image are observable-law functionals.  Positive covariate-cell support and treatment overlap give
\[
 \Pr_P(Z=z,X=x)>0
 \qquad(z\in\{0,1\},\ x\in\mathcal X),
\]
and full-horizon censoring support gives \(G_{zx}(L)\geq\gamma>0\).  Thus all conditioning and inverse weights in the established IPCW-recovery lemma are well defined.  By that lemma, consistency, conditional exchangeability, arm-specific independent censoring, and the two support assumptions identify \(\mu_{zx}\), including its atom at \(\infty\).  Marginalization and integration then identify \(d_x\), \(\zeta_x\), \(b_x\), \(K_x\), \(s_x\), and \(S\).

For necessity, fix \(Q_x\in\mathcal Q_x\), and let \(\nu_x\) be its \((D(0),R(1))\)-margin.  Its margins are \(d_x\) and \(\zeta_x\).  For every \(u\in[0,\tau]\) and Borel \(B\subseteq\mathcal E\), terminal monotonicity gives the event inclusion
\[
 \{D(0)>u,R(1)\in B\}
 \subseteq
 \{D(1)>u,R(1)\in B\}.
\]
Taking \(Q_x\)-probabilities and using the treated within-arm margin gives
\[
 \nu_x((u,\infty]\times B)
 \leq \mu_{1x}(D(1)>u,R(1)\in B)
 =K_x(u,B).
\]
This holds for every mark set \(B\), not merely for the unmarked survival margin, and hence \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\) by the survivor-capacity definition.

For sufficiency, fix \(x\) and \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\).  Regard \(\alpha=\nu_x\) and \(\beta=\mu_{1x}\) as probability measures on two copies of \(\mathcal E^2\); their second-coordinate margins both equal \(\zeta_x\).  Introduce the closed relation
\[
 \mathcal R
 =\{((d_0,v),(d_1,v')):v=v',\ d_0\leq d_1\}.
\]
It is closed because the diagonal and the order graph are closed in the compact metric carrier \(\mathcal E\).

We verify the compact-set inequalities in the established Strassen closed-relation lemma.  The capacity inequalities imply
\[
 \alpha([u,\infty]\times B)\leq\beta([u,\infty]\times B)
 \qquad(u\in\mathcal E,\ B\in\mathscr B(\mathcal E)).                 \tag{1}
\]
For \(0<u\leq\tau\), choose \(u_k\uparrow u\) with \(u_k<u\), apply the defining inequality to \((u_k,\infty]\times B\), and use continuity from above.  At \(u=0\), (1) is equality because the second margins coincide.  At \(u=\infty\), (1) is the boundary cut \((\tau,\infty]=\{\infty\}\), so the horizon atom is included.

Let \(A\subseteq\mathcal E^2\) be compact and put \(U=\mathcal R(A)\), viewing \(U\) as a subset of the second copy of \(\mathcal E^2\).  Compactness of \(A\), closedness of \(\mathcal R\), and compactness of the product imply that \(U\) is compact.  For each mark \(v\), its section is empty or a closed upper interval \([h(v),\infty]\).  For finite \(a\),
\[
 \{v:h(v)\leq a\}
 =\operatorname{proj}_v\!\left(A\cap([0,a]\times\mathcal E)\right),
\]
which is compact; hence \(h\) is Borel measurable on the nonempty sections.  On nested finite grids of \([0,\tau]\), round each finite \(h(v)\) down to \(\underline h_n(v)\), while retaining the \(\infty\) and empty sections.  The resulting \(U_n\) decrease to \(U\), and every \(U_n\) is a finite disjoint union of sets \([q,\infty]\times B_{nq}\), with Borel, pairwise disjoint mark sets \(B_{nq}\).  Summing (1) over these disjoint pieces and passing to the decreasing limit yields
\[
 \alpha(A)\leq\alpha(U)\leq\beta(U)=\beta(\mathcal R(A)).             \tag{2}
\]
The Strassen lemma applied to (2) supplies a coupling of \((D(0),R(1))\sim\nu_x\) and \((D(1),R'(1))\sim\mu_{1x}\) supported on \(R(1)=R'(1)\) and \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  Identifying the equal mark coordinates gives a law \(\pi_x\) of \((D(0),D(1),R(1))\).

Reorder \(\mu_{0x}\) as the law of \((R(0),D(0))\).  This law and \(\pi_x\) have the same \(D(0)\)-margin \(d_x\).  The established compact-coordinate gluing lemma therefore gives a law \(Q_x\) of \((R(0),D(0),D(1),R(1))\) satisfying
\[
 \mathcal L_{Q_x}(D(0),R(0))=\mu_{0x},\qquad
 \mathcal L_{Q_x}(D(1),R(1))=\mu_{1x},\qquad
 Q_x\{D(0)\leq D(1)\}=1.                                            \tag{3}
\]
The within-arm strict event orders are inherited from the fixed margins.  No density or rank condition is used in this lift.

Because \(\mathcal X\) is finite, \(x\mapsto Q_x\) is automatically a measurable probability kernel.  Draw \(X\) with masses \(p_x\); conditionally on \(X=x\), draw the potential path from \(Q_x\), draw \(Z\) independently of that path with probability \(e(x)\), and draw \(C\) from its observed conditional law given \((Z,X)\), independently of the potential path.  Consistency forms the factual event path.  Equation (3) gives exactly \(\mu_{zx}\) in arm \(z\) and cell \(x\), while the construction preserves the observed laws of \((X,Z,C)\).  Arm-specific independent censoring makes the corresponding conditional observed-history factorization the same as under \(P\).  Since \(O\) is a measurable function of these variables, the lifted law reproduces \(P\).

It remains to relate the causal targets to the observed-law image.  Terminal monotonicity gives
\[
 \{D(0)>t,D(1)>t\}=\{D(0)>t\}.                                      \tag{4}
\]
For \((r,t)\in\mathcal H_\eta\), the target-domain definition gives \(S(t)\geq\eta>0\), so conditioning is legitimate.  Conditioning first on \(X\), and using (4), \(\nu_x\), and \(b_x\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr\{R(1)\leq r\mid D(0)>t,D(1)>t\}
-\Pr\{R(0)\leq r\mid D(0)>t,D(1)>t\}\\
&\quad=\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x
 \{\nu_x((t,\infty]\times[0,r])-b_x(r,t)\}}{S(t)}
=\theta_\nu(r,t).                                                    \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(q\in\mathcal E\) and \(0\leq a\leq t\), including \(q=\infty\),
\[
 \min\{q,a\}=a-\int_0^a\mathbf 1\{q\leq r\}\,dr.
\]
Integrating this bounded identity under the two conditional laws, subtracting, and using (5) yields
\[
 E[\min\{R(1),a\}-\min\{R(0),a\}\mid D(0)>t,D(1)>t]
 =-\int_0^a\theta_\nu(r,t)\,dr
 =\rho_\nu(a,t).                                                     \tag{6}
\]

Necessity puts every compatible causal surface in \(\Theta_I(P)\); the measurable construction attains every member of that image while preserving all maintained restrictions and \(P\).  Equations (5)--(6) prove, rather than define, the equality with the causal target.  Thus the characterization is sharp for the nonparametric class with \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  If terminal monotonicity is removed, both the necessity inclusion and (4) can fail, so no equality for that larger class follows.

The proof is a conservation reduction followed by finite linear-program duality.  Fix \(x\) and suppress it temporarily.  Index ordered death categories by \(i=0,\ldots,m\), with the last category representing \(\infty\).  A projected table has the required margins exactly when
\[
 \sum_j f_{ij}=d_x(i),\qquad \sum_i f_{ij}=\zeta_x(j).                \tag{7}
\]
On the finite carrier, the survivor-capacity inequality for the singleton mark \(\{j\}\) is
\[
 \sum_{i>k}f_{ij}\leq
 \mu_{1x}(D(1)>k,R(1)=j)=\kappa^x_{kj}.                              \tag{8}
\]
Summing (8) over \(j\) in an arbitrary grid mark set proves every marked-capacity inequality; conversely, singleton sets recover (8).  Thus (7), (8), and nonnegativity are equivalent to \(f^x\in\mathcal N_x\) by the survivor-capacity definition.

For each mark \(j\), create chain nodes \(v_{0j},\ldots,v_{mj}\), inject \(\zeta_x(j)\) at \(v_{0j}\), put an exit of size \(f_{ij}\) from \(v_{ij}\) to death-demand node \(i\), and give the arc \(v_{kj}\to v_{k+1,j}\) capacity \(\kappa^x_{kj}\).  Conservation through the first \(k+1\) nodes forces the chain-arc load to equal
\[
 q_{kj}=\zeta_x(j)-\sum_{i\leq k}f_{ij}
 =\sum_{i>k}f_{ij}.                                                   \tag{9}
\]
Equations (7)--(8) therefore turn a feasible table into a feasible chain flow.  Conversely, the exit flows of a feasible network obey (7), and (9) with the arc capacities gives (8).  With \(m\) levels on each axis, the construction has \(O(m^2)\) chain nodes, exit arcs, and capacity arcs.  The full-law lift is the finite specialization of the proved capacity-projection theorem, whose hypotheses include terminal monotonicity and the within-arm semicompeting order.

For the support value in one cell, write the primal as
\[
 \max_{f\geq0}\ \sum_{i,j}c^x_{ij}f_{ij}
\]
subject to (7)--(8).  Put free multipliers \(\alpha_i,\beta_j\) on the two families of margin equalities and nonnegative multipliers \(\lambda_{kj}\) on (8).  If
\[
 \alpha_i+\beta_j+\sum_{k<i}\lambda_{kj}\geq c^x_{ij},
 \qquad \lambda_{kj}\geq0,                                          \tag{10}
\]
then every primal-feasible \(f\) satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i,j}c^x_{ij}f_{ij}
 &\leq\sum_{i,j}\left(\alpha_i+\beta_j+
        \sum_{k<i}\lambda_{kj}\right)f_{ij}\\
 &=\sum_i\alpha_i d_x(i)+\sum_j\beta_j\zeta_x(j)
   +\sum_{k,j}\lambda_{kj}\sum_{i>k}f_{ij}\\
 &\leq\sum_i\alpha_i d_x(i)+\sum_j\beta_j\zeta_x(j)
   +\sum_{k,j}\lambda_{kj}\kappa^x_{kj}.                            \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
This is weak duality for precisely the node-potential program in the grid-support definition.  The primal feasible set is a closed subset of a finite probability simplex, hence compact, and its signed objective is bounded.  The established finite LP strong-duality lemma makes (11) an equality at the optima and gives attainment.  Constraints do not share unknowns across \(x\), so the support of the product fiber is the sum of its cellwise supports, which is exactly \(h_m(c)\).

The proof uses nested-deadline matching, suffix cuts, and compact limiting.  Fix \(x\) and \(t\), write \(s=s_x(t)\), and extend the treated survivor kernel by the boundary convention \(K_x(\infty,B)=0\).  If \(s=0\), the cut at \(\infty\) makes both deadline ranks zero, and the assertion is immediate.  Assume henceforth that \(s>0\).

For any compatible full law, let \(w\) be the treated-record submeasure selected by \(D(0)>t\):
\[
 w(H)=\Pr\{(D(1),R(1))\in H,D(0)>t\mid X=x\}.
\]
It has mass \(s\), is dominated by \(\mu_{1x}\), is supported on \(D(1)>t\), and terminal monotonicity gives, for every \(u\geq t\),
\[
 w(D(1)>u)\geq\Pr(D(0)>u\mid X=x)=s_x(u).                             \tag{12}
\]
For a Borel mark set \(B\), split selected records at deadline \(u\).  At most \(s-s_x(u)\) selected records can lie at or before \(u\), by (12), and at most \(K_x(u,B)\) available \(B\)-records lie after \(u\).  Hence
\[
 w(R(1)\in B)\leq s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,B),
\]
including the boundary cut \(u=\infty\).  Taking the infimum proves the upper deadline bound.

We next prove sharpness on a finite rational grid.  Multiply all masses by a common denominator.  Make one demand copy for each unit of control mass with \(D(0)>t\), and one resource copy for each unit of treated mass with \(D(1)>t\).  Join a demand of death level \(i\) to a resource of level \(h\) exactly when \(i\leq h\).  Taking the full mark set in the capacity inequalities gives every suffix inequality
\[
 \#\{\text{resources of level greater than }u\}
 \geq \#\{\text{demands of level greater than }u\}.                \tag{13}
\]
Sorting demands from latest to earliest and assigning at each step an unused admissible resource proves by induction from (13) that all demands can be matched.

For resources whose marks lie in \(B\), run the usual alternating-path augmentation, which is elementary here because neighborhoods are nested suffixes.  If augmentation stops, the demands reachable by alternating paths may be replaced by the suffix beginning at their earliest death level without enlarging their resource neighborhood.  Absence of an augmenting path then partitions every matched \(B\)-resource into either a resource used by a demand outside that suffix or a \(B\)-resource adjacent to the suffix.  At the stopping suffix \(u\), equality holds in
\[
 \#\{\text{matched \(B\)-resources}\}
 \leq \#\{\text{demands at or before }u\}
      +\#\{\text{available \(B\)-resources after }u\}.             \tag{14}
\]
The right side is the scaled value \(s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,B)\).  Conversely, (14) is valid for every matching and every suffix, as already proved.  Thus the maximum number of selected \(B\)-resources equals the minimum deadline cut.  Superposing a maximizing partial matching with a full matching and augmenting along their alternating paths and cycles extends it to a full matching without deleting a selected \(B\)-resource.

The matchable subsets of resources satisfy augmentation: if one matchable set is smaller than another, superpose their matchings; an alternating path starting from a resource used only by the larger matching augments the smaller one.  Order resources by increasing readmission category and greedily accept a resource whenever the accepted set remains matchable.  After every prefix, augmentation implies that the accepted set has maximum possible size within that prefix.  Extending the final accepted set to a matching of all survivor demands gives one selected submeasure that attains the deadline-cut maximum simultaneously for every readmission prefix.  Reversing the mark order maximizes every complementary suffix and therefore simultaneously minimizes every prefix.

It remains to pair the unselected treated records with the control deaths at or before \(t\).  Write \(T_x(u)=\Pr(D(1)>u\mid X=x)\).  For \(u\leq t\), every selected resource has \(D(1)>t\), so its tail mass at \(u\) is \(s\); the residual treated tail is \(T_x(u)-s\), whereas the residual control tail is \(s_x(u)-s\).  Marginal terminal dominance, obtained by taking the full mark set in the survivor-capacity inequality, gives
\[
 T_x(u)-s\geq s_x(u)-s.
\]
For \(u>t\), the residual control tail is zero.  Sorting both residual collections from latest to earliest and applying the same suffix induction therefore completes the matching without changing the selected cohort.  Thus every extremizing selected matching extends to a full terminal-monotone coupling.

For arbitrary real finite masses, approximate the complete finite table by rational tables on the same allowed cells.  The rational extremizers lie in a fixed finite simplex.  A convergent subsequence preserves nonnegativity, both margins, and the closed order constraint, while every finite cut and objective converges.  This proves the same formula and common-prefix conclusion for real finite tables.

For continuous time, take nested finite partitions containing \(t\) and any prescribed finite collection of readmission thresholds, isolate \(\infty\), and retain the within-cell order relation.  Apply the finite result to the coarsened margins and take full-law lifts furnished by the quadratic chain theorem.  The compact-carrier lemma gives a weakly convergent subsequence.  Its limit has the original within-arm margins and the closed order \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The density envelope implies zero mass at every finite threshold and, for \(u<v\),
\[
 |K_x(u,B)-K_x(v,B)|
 \leq\Pr\{u<D(1)\leq v\mid X=x\}\leq M|u-v|.                       \tag{15}
\]
The analogous bound holds for \(s_x\).  Consequently the discrete suffix minima converge to the continuum infimum, and the limiting coupling attains the extrema at every threshold in the prescribed finite collection.

Inside the compact fixed-margin full-law fiber, the set of couplings attaining the upper value at a given finite \(r\) is closed: the objective boundary is contained in \(\{D(0)=t\}\cup\{R(1)=r\}\), which has probability zero by the fixed finite-part marginal densities.  The preceding finite-threshold construction gives these closed optimizing sets the finite-intersection property.  Compactness therefore supplies one coupling attaining the upper value for every \(r\leq t\).  Reversing the readmission order supplies one lower coupling for all such \(r\).

Taking \(B=[0,r]\) identifies the upper endpoint as \(A_x^U(r,t)\).  Applying the upper formula to \(B=(r,\infty]\) and subtracting from the total selected mass gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \min_\nu\nu_x(D(0)>t,R(1)\leq r)
 &=s-\inf_u\{s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,(r,\infty])\}\\
 &=\sup_u\{s_x(u)-K_x(u,(r,\infty])\}=A_x^L(r,t).                   \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
For a fixed cohort \(t\), choose the common extremizer separately in each of the finitely many covariate cells.  Since \(p_x/S(t)\geq0\) and \(S(t)\geq\eta>0\) on the target domain, summing the cell endpoints and subtracting the fixed \(b_x(r,t)\) gives the sharp standardized TV-SACE envelopes \(\theta^L\) and \(\theta^U\).

Finally, every compatible surface obeys \(\theta^L(r,t)\leq\theta_\nu(r,t)\leq\theta^U(r,t)\).  The RM-surface definition gives
\[
 -\int_0^a\theta^U(r,t)\,dr
 \leq\rho_\nu(a,t)\leq
 -\int_0^a\theta^L(r,t)\,dr.                                       \tag{17}
\]
The common upper and lower couplings attain the left and right endpoints of (17), respectively.  Thus fixed-cohort RM integration is sharp because of common extremizers, not merely because every TV coordinate is separately sharp.

The proof is an exact finite-table certificate followed by separated smoothing.  All probabilities are conditional on the sole value of \(X\).  Since \(R(0)=\infty\), the control numerator is \(b(r,t)=0\) at finite \(r\).  The four control death rows each have mass \(1/4\), so
\[
 S(1)=\frac34,\qquad S(2)=\frac12,\qquad S(3)=\frac14.               \tag{18}
\]
Thus \(0<\eta\leq1/4\) places \((1,1),(2,2),(3,3)\) in \(\mathcal H_\eta\), including its boundary.

For a feasible projected table \(f=(f_{ij})\), define
\[
 A_1=\sum_{i>0}f_{i0},\qquad
 A_2=\sum_{\substack{i>1\\j\leq1}}f_{ij},\qquad
 A_3=\sum_{j\leq2}f_{3j}.
\]
The singleton capacities from the quadratic chain theorem and the fixed row demands give
\[
 \frac1{20}\leq A_1\leq\kappa^\star_{00}=\frac15,                  \tag{19}
\]
because the other three first-cut columns have total capacity \(7/10\), while the demand after that cut is \(3/4\).  Similarly,
\[
 \frac1{20}\leq A_2\leq\kappa^\star_{10}+\kappa^\star_{11}
 =\frac14,                                                            \tag{20}
\]
because the second-cut demand is \(1/2\) and columns \(2,3\) have capacity \(9/20\).  Finally,
\[
 \frac1{20}\leq A_3\leq
 \kappa^\star_{20}+\kappa^\star_{21}+\kappa^\star_{22}=\frac15,    \tag{21}
\]
where the lower bound is \(A_3=1/4-f_{33}\geq1/4-\kappa^\star_{23}\).

The upper endpoints in (19)--(21) are attained by the displayed flows \(f^+\), \(f^-\), and \(f^+\), respectively, and the lower endpoint in (21) is attained by \(f^-\).  For the remaining lower endpoints, define
\[
100g^{(1)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\0&15&5&5\\0&0&5&20\\5&5&5&10
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
100g^{(2)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\0&20&0&5\\0&0&10&15\\5&0&5&15
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both have the required row and column margins.  Their complete singleton chain loads are
\[
\begin{pmatrix}5&20&15&35\\5&5&10&30\\5&5&5&10\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\begin{pmatrix}5&20&15&35\\5&0&15&30\\5&0&5&15\end{pmatrix},
\]
after multiplication by \(100\); each is entrywise bounded by \(100\kappa^\star\).  The quadratic chain theorem makes both flows feasible, with \(A_1(g^{(1)})=1/20\) and \(A_2(g^{(2)})=1/20\).  Convexity of the finite flow polytope then shows that (19)--(21) are the exact intervals.  Dividing by (18) gives
\[
 \theta_\nu(1,1)\in\left[\frac1{15},\frac4{15}\right],\quad
 \theta_\nu(2,2)\in\left[\frac1{10},\frac12\right],\quad
 \theta_\nu(3,3)\in\left[\frac15,\frac45\right].                  \tag{22}
\]

Direct summation of the listed nonzero lift entries gives
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^-_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=\begin{pmatrix}10&0&10&5\\0&10&5&10\\15&5&0&5\\0&5&0&20\end{pmatrix}
=100f^-,
\]
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^+_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=\begin{pmatrix}5&0&10&10\\10&15&0&0\\0&0&0&25\\10&5&5&5\end{pmatrix}
=100f^+,
\]
and, for both signs,
\[
100\left(\sum_iq^\pm_{ihj}\right)_{hj}
=\begin{pmatrix}5&0&0&5\\5&10&0&5\\5&5&10&10\\10&5&5&20\end{pmatrix}
=100\mu_1^\star.
\]
Every listed entry is nonnegative.  Both projected tables have row sums \((25,25,25,25)/100\) and column sums \((25,20,15,40)/100\), so attaching \(R(0)=\infty\) gives \(\mu_0^\star\).  Inspection of every positive triple gives \(i\leq h\), hence \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  Every finite treated readmission category in a positive cell satisfies \(r_j^\star<d_h^\star\), while the control event order is vacuous.  The complete singleton chain loads are
\[
100\left(\sum_{i>k}f^-_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=\begin{pmatrix}15&20&5&35\\15&10&0&25\\0&5&0&20\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
100\left(\sum_{i>k}f^+_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=\begin{pmatrix}20&20&5&30\\10&5&5&30\\10&5&5&5\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Comparison with the displayed \(100\kappa^\star\) is entrywise.  Every Borel mark set on this finite carrier is a union of singleton columns, so summing these inequalities certifies all event-set capacities.

Substituting (18) into the signed direction yields
\[
 \ell_\star(\nu)=A_1-A_2+A_3=f_{10}-f_{21}+f_{30}+f_{32}.            \tag{23}
\]
Nonnegativity and the first and third cut capacities give
\[
 \ell_\star(\nu)
 \leq f_{10}+f_{30}+f_{32}
 \leq\kappa^\star_{00}+\kappa^\star_{22}=\frac14.                  \tag{24}
\]
The second-cut capacity in column \(1\) and the last-row margin give
\[
 f_{21}+f_{31}\leq\frac1{10},\qquad
 f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32}=\frac14-f_{33}\geq\frac1{20}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \ell_\star(\nu)
 =f_{10}-(f_{21}+f_{31})+(f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32})
 \geq-\frac1{20}.                                                     \tag{25}
\]
Direct substitution gives \(\ell_\star(f^-)=-1/20\) and \(\ell_\star(f^+)=1/4\).  The verified full lifts attain both values, and mixtures of them preserve the fixed margins, monotonicity, and event order.  Hence the sharp signed interval is \([-1/20,1/4]\).

If the three coordinates in (22) could vary independently, the same direction would instead have endpoints
\[
 \frac34\frac1{15}-\frac12\frac12+\frac14\frac15=-\frac3{20},
 \qquad
 \frac34\frac4{15}-\frac12\frac1{10}+\frac14\frac45=\frac7{20}.
\]
Thus the coordinate rectangle has support \([-3/20,7/20]\), strictly larger by \(1/10\) at each endpoint.

For smoothing, choose a nonnegative symmetric continuously differentiable density \(\varphi_\delta\) of integral one supported on \((-\delta,\delta)\), where \(0<\delta<1/8\).  Replace every finite category by the corresponding translated bump and retain \(\infty\).  Conditional on a positive categorical lift cell \((i,h,j)\), use independent death bumps when \(i<h\), the same death draw when \(i=h\), and an independent readmission bump.  Adjacent death centers are one unit apart, so this preserves \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The smallest finite gap between a compatible treated readmission center and death center is \(1/4\), and \(2\delta<1/4\) therefore preserves \(R(1)<D(1)\).  Finite-part within-arm densities are finite mixtures of translates and products of \(\varphi_\delta\), so they have finite sup-norm and Lipschitz constants and meet the audited envelopes whenever those constants are chosen as the corresponding model bounds.

No bump support crosses any threshold \(1,2,3\).  All numerators, denominators, and capacities used in (19)--(25) therefore retain their categorical values.  Applying the same bump kernels under the two signs preserves their common smoothed within-arm margins, while the two projected couplings retain the two signed endpoints.  The exact support calculations thus remain valid for bounded-Lipschitz witnesses.

Finally fix the separated kernels and incidence pattern and vary the finitely many mixture weights inside the feasible cone.  After slack variables are introduced, the support programs have a fixed finite constraint matrix and finitely many bases.  On every basis region the optimal value is affine in the weights, and values agree where optimality regions meet; hence every endpoint is continuous and piecewise affine.  Both strict gaps equal \(1/10\) at the displayed law, so they remain positive on a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood.  The randomized treatment \(e=1/2\), degenerate positive covariate cell, consistency, and \(C=\tau=3\) additionally give exchangeability, overlap, and \(G_{zx}(u)=1\geq\gamma\) through the full horizon.

The proof uses weak compactness, a common modulus, and two-sided approximation of feasible fibers.  Fix the identified within-arm margins.  For each \(x\), let \(\mathcal Q_x\) be the full-law fiber with these margins and support on \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The compact-carrier lemma makes the ambient probability-law space weakly compact.  Marginalization is weakly continuous, and the monotonicity relation is closed; hence \(\mathcal Q_x\) is closed and compact.  The strict within-arm event order causes no closure problem because every law in the fiber has the same fixed margins, each supported on the semicompeting-risk set.  The capacity-projection theorem identifies the \((D(0),R(1))\)-projection of \(\mathcal Q_x\) with \(\mathcal N_x\).  Therefore every \(\mathcal N_x\), and their finite product over \(\mathcal X\), is compact and convex.

For \(r,r',t,t'\in[0,\tau]\) and \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\), the fixed death and readmission margins imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|\nu_x((t,\infty]\times[0,r])
-\nu_x((t',\infty]\times[0,r'])\right|\\
&\qquad\leq d_x((t\wedge t',t\vee t'])
+\zeta_x((r\wedge r',r\vee r'])
\leq M(|t-t'|+|r-r'|).                                                \tag{26}
\end{aligned}
\]
The density envelope gives the analogous bound for \(b_x\), and \(|S(t)-S(t')|\leq M|t-t'|\).  On \(\mathcal H_\eta\), \(S\geq\eta>0\), while every numerator is bounded in absolute value by one.  Thus
\[
 \left|\frac{N}{S}-\frac{N'}{S'}\right|
 \leq\frac{|N-N'|}{\eta}
 +\frac{|N'|\,|S-S'|}{\eta^2}                                       \tag{27}
\]
gives one Lipschitz modulus for all \(\theta_\nu\).  The same density bound makes \(S\) continuous, so the target-domain definition makes \(\mathcal H_\eta\) a closed subset of the compact time triangle.  Integrating the common TV modulus gives a common modulus for \(\rho_\nu\).

If \(\nu_x^{(q)}\Rightarrow\nu_x\), each finite threshold rectangle in the surface formula is a continuity set because the fixed finite-part death and readmission margins have densities.  Hence \(\theta_{\nu^{(q)}}\to\theta_\nu\) pointwise.  Equation (27) and a finite net of the compact target domain upgrade pointwise convergence to uniform convergence.  The RM integral then converges uniformly as well.  Thus the surface map is continuous from a compact fiber into \(C(\mathcal H_\eta)^2\).  Its image \(\Theta_I(P)\) is compact.  It is convex because the TV numerator and RM integral are affine in \(\nu\), while \(S\) and \(b_x\) are fixed.  Every continuous linear signed support functional therefore attains both extrema.

Now take nested partitions of mesh \(\delta_m\downarrow0\) that isolate \(\infty\), round finite death coordinates monotonically upward, retain within-bin event-order labels, and use one fixed multilinear interpolation on the triangular domain.  Let \(K_m\) be the exact chain-flow surface image for the coarsened fixed margins and let \(K=\Theta_I(P)\).  For any \(Q\in\prod_x\mathcal Q_x\), coarsening all finite coordinates preserves every suffix capacity because \(D(0)>u\) still implies \(D(1)>u\).  At grid knots the coarsened and continuous numerators can differ only on boundary strips of width at most \(\delta_m\), whose marginal probability is at most \(M\delta_m\) per coordinate.  Upward death rounding gives a coarsened survivor denominator no smaller than \(S\), and its difference from \(S\) is at most \(M\delta_m\).  Equation (27) and interpolation therefore give a constant \(C=C(M,\eta,\tau,|\mathcal X|)\) such that
\[
 \sup_{q\in K}\inf_{q_m\in K_m}\|q-q_m\|_\infty
 \leq C\delta_m\longrightarrow0.                                   \tag{28}
\]

Conversely, take \(q_m\in K_m\) and use the quadratic chain theorem to lift its grid flow to a finite-grid full law.  Embed every finite category at a legal representative in its cell, using the retained order label when two events share a cell.  The embedded within-arm margins converge weakly to the fixed margins.  Grid monotonicity gives \(D_m(0)\leq D_m(1)+\delta_m\), so every weak subsequential limit is supported on the closed relation \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  Compactness supplies such a subsequence, and its limit lies in \(\prod_x\mathcal Q_x\).

Every finite grid atom is bounded by the fixed marginal mass of one mesh cell and hence by \(M\delta_m\).  The interpolated grid surfaces therefore obey the common modulus (26)--(27), up to a term vanishing with \(\delta_m\).  Pointwise convergence at continuity thresholds and the finite-net argument show that the chosen subsequence converges uniformly to the surface of its limiting compatible law.  If the reverse directed distance did not vanish, a countersequence attaining a positive lower bound and this subsequence construction would contradict that bound.  Hence
\[
 \sup_{q_m\in K_m}\inf_{q\in K}\|q_m-q\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.    \tag{29}
\]
Equations (28)--(29) prove \(d_H(K_m,K)\to0\).

For every continuous linear functional \(L\),
\[
 \left|\sup_{q_m\in K_m}L(q_m)-\sup_{q\in K}L(q)\right|
 \leq\|L\|\,d_H(K_m,K)\longrightarrow0.                            \tag{30}
\]
The fixed-cohort theorem expresses the sharp RM endpoints as integrals of common sharp TV envelopes.  Their common modulus and Hausdorff convergence yield uniform convergence of those envelopes, so
\[
 \left|\int_0^a\theta_m^{U,L}(r,t)\,dr
-\int_0^a\theta^{U,L}(r,t)\,dr\right|
\leq a\,\|\theta_m^{U,L}-\theta^{U,L}\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus exact grid supports and sharp fixed-cohort RM integrals converge to their continuous-support counterparts.

The proof combines a conditional exponential-moment inequality with deterministic propagation through the observable moment region.  If \(B\in\{0,1\}\) has mean \(q\), let \(\psi(\lambda)=\log E\exp\{\lambda(B-q)\}\).  Exponential tilting preserves a Bernoulli law, so \(\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0\) and \(\psi''(\lambda)=q_\lambda(1-q_\lambda)\leq1/4\).  Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives
\[
 E\exp\{\lambda(B-q)\}\leq\exp(\lambda^2/8).
\]
For \(N>0\) independent copies, Markov's inequality and optimization at \(\lambda=4r\) yield
\[
 \Pr(|\bar B_N-q|>r)\leq2e^{-2Nr^2}.                                \tag{31}
\]

Conditional on all treatment--covariate cell counts, observations in each nonempty cell are independent draws from its conditional cell law.  With
\[
 r_{zx}=\sqrt{\frac{\log(2J/\alpha)}{2N_{zx}}},
\]
equation (31) bounds each two-sided primitive-interval failure probability by \(\alpha/J\).  The same calculation with \(N=n\) applies to every \(\widehat p_x\).  An interval in a zero-count cell is \([0,1]\) and cannot fail.  Since \(J\) counts all primitive and covariate-mass intervals, a union bound conditional on the counts, followed by averaging over them, gives
\[
 \inf_P\Pr_P(\mathscr E_n)\geq1-\alpha.                             \tag{32}
\]
Treatment overlap and positive covariate-cell support, the latter inherited through the IPCW-recovery dependency, ensure that every population conditional cell law used here is well defined; no lower bound on realized counts is required.

Fix \((z,x)\).  Arm-specific independent censoring gives
\[
 A^{zx}_{ij}=\int_{I_i\times B_j}G_{zx}(d)\,\mu_{zx}(d d,d r).
\]
Since \(G_{zx}\) is nonincreasing and \(a_i\leq d<a_{i+1}\),
\[
 g^{zx}_{i+1}\pi^{zx}_{ij}\leq A^{zx}_{ij}
 \leq g^{zx}_i\pi^{zx}_{ij}.                                       \tag{33}
\]
For an exact discrete death grid, the censoring survival is evaluated at the unique grid death time and (33) is the equality stipulated in the outer-set definition.  Independence at deterministic times \(a_i\) and \(\tau\) similarly gives
\[
 Y^{zx}_i=g^{zx}_i\left\{\sum_{h\geq i,j}\pi^{zx}_{hj}
 +\sum_j\pi^{zx}_{\infty j}\right\},\qquad
 V^{zx}_j=g^{zx}_m\pi^{zx}_{\infty j}.                              \tag{34}
\]
By the survival-function definition and full-horizon support,
\[
 1\geq g^{zx}_0\geq\cdots\geq g^{zx}_m\geq\gamma>0.                \tag{35}
\]
The true tables obey the simplex and inherited semicompeting event-order restrictions.  On \(\mathscr E_n\), every true observable moment and every \(p_x\) lies in its stipulated interval.  Equations (33)--(35) therefore place the true coarsened primitive vector and censoring vector in \(\mathcal B_n\).

Take any surface in \(\Theta_I(P)\), restrict it to \(\mathcal G_m\), and coarsen each projected coupling into the same death and mark bins.  Its margins are the true coarsened \(d_x\) and \(\zeta_x\), and for every cut and mark bin,
\[
 \sum_{i>k}f^x_{ij}
 =\nu_x(D(0)>a_k,R(1)\in B_j)
 \leq K_x(a_k,B_j)=\kappa^x_{kj}.                                   \tag{36}
\]
The quadratic chain theorem makes (36) an exact grid surface in the image attached to the true primitive vector.  Since that vector lies in \(\mathcal B_n\) on \(\mathscr E_n\), the union defining \(\mathcal C_n\) gives
\[
 \Theta_I(P)|_{\mathcal G_m}\subseteq\mathcal C_n
 \qquad\text{on }\mathscr E_n.                                     \tag{37}
\]
Combining (32) and (37) proves the claimed uniform \(1-\alpha\) outer containment.  The argument propagates a single simultaneous primitive event and never differentiates an optimal flow face, so ties and changes of active cuts do not affect validity.

Assume \(D(0)=D(1)\) almost surely in the compatible full-law class.  For \(x\in\mathcal X\), \(t\in[0,\tau]\), and Borel \(B\subseteq\mathcal E\), define finite measures
\[
 q_{x,t}(B)=\nu_x((t,\infty]\times B),\qquad
 k_{x,t}(B)=\mu_{1x}(D(1)>t,R(1)\in B).
\]
The survivor-capacity definition gives \(q_{x,t}(B)\leq k_{x,t}(B)\).  Equality of the death variables, and hence their identified margins, gives
\[
 q_{x,t}(\mathcal E)=d_x((t,\infty])
 =\Pr(D(1)>t\mid X=x)=k_{x,t}(\mathcal E).                           \tag{38}
\]
Applying capacity to \(B^c\) and subtracting from (38) gives
\[
 q_{x,t}(B)
 =q_{x,t}(\mathcal E)-q_{x,t}(B^c)
 \geq k_{x,t}(\mathcal E)-k_{x,t}(B^c)=k_{x,t}(B).
\]
Thus the two finite measures are equal, and in particular
\[
 \nu_x(D(0)>t,R(1)\leq r)
 =\mu_{1x}(D(1)>t,R(1)\leq r).                                      \tag{39}
\]
The IPCW-recovery lemma identifies both within-arm laws, while the TV-surface definition uses only (39), the identified control term \(b_x\), the weights \(p_x\), and \(S(t)>0\) on the target domain.  Hence \(\theta_\nu\) is independent of \(\nu\); the RM definition makes \(\rho_\nu\) independent of \(\nu\) as well.  The capacity-projection theorem says every compatible surface is represented in this fiber, so \(\Theta_I(P)\) is the singleton ordinary standardized within-arm cumulative-incidence contrast among the common survivor cohort.

The finite-table certificate in the strict-support proposition gives
\[
 \left(\sum_hq^-_{ihj}\right)_{ij}=f^-_{ij},\qquad
 \left(\sum_hq^+_{ihj}\right)_{ij}=f^+_{ij},\qquad
 \left(\sum_iq^-_{ihj}\right)_{hj}
 =\left(\sum_iq^+_{ihj}\right)_{hj}=\mu_{1,hj}^\star.                \tag{40}
\]
After attaching \(R(0)=\infty\), both laws have control margin \(\mu_0^\star\).  Every listed positive entry has \(i\leq h\), so both laws satisfy \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  They are distinct because, for example,
\[
 f^-_{00}=\frac1{10}\neq\frac1{20}=f^+_{00}.                         \tag{41}
\]
The strict-support proposition computes \(S(1)=3/4\), \(S(2)=1/2\), and \(S(3)=1/4\).  The premise \(0<\eta\leq1/4\) therefore ensures that all three coordinates in \(\ell_\star\), including \(\theta_\nu(3,3)\), belong to \(\mathcal H_\eta\).

The construction uses under both signs the same degenerate covariate, \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) independent of the potential path, and \(C=\tau=3\).  By consistency, arm \(z\) reveals only \((D(z),R(z))\).  Thus, for every measurable observed-path set \(A\), if \(\mathcal O(z,d,r,3)\) is the deterministic observed history generated by these inputs, then
\[
 \Pr_\pm(O\in A)
 =\frac12\sum_{z=0}^1
   \int\mathbf 1\{\mathcal O(z,d,r,3)\in A\}\,d\mu_z^\star(d,r),  \tag{42}
\]
which is independent of the sign.  This construction directly satisfies conditional exchangeability; \(e=1/2\) and \(G_z(u)=1\) verify treatment overlap and censoring support through \(\tau\).  The strict-support proposition computes
\[
 \ell_\star(f^-)=-\frac1{20},\qquad
 \ell_\star(f^+)=\frac14.                                           \tag{43}
\]

Let \(\mathfrak C\) be any causal class containing both atomic laws.  At the common observable distribution in (42), its identified set for \(\ell_\star\) contains both values in (43), whose difference is \(3/10>0\).  Hence \(\ell_\star\) is not point identified in \(\mathfrak C\), and neither is the joint surface pair.  Enlarging a model class can only retain these compatible witnesses.  This inclusion argument says nothing about whether additional, possibly nonmonotone laws are represented by \(\mathcal N_x\), and therefore proves no enlarged-class sharpness claim.

added_lemmas.statement: Suppose \(0<\eta\leq1/4\).  Apply the same sufficiently narrow separated bump kernels to the two full laws \(q^-_{ihj}\) and \(q^+_{ihj}\) in \(\mathfrak E_3\).  The resulting two bounded-Lipschitz full laws satisfy the maintained event-order and terminal-monotonicity restrictions, have identical smoothed control and treated within-arm laws, and induce the same observable distribution under the common randomized treatment and full-horizon censoring mechanisms.  Their values of \(\ell_\star\) remain \(-1/20\) and \(1/4\).  Hence every maintained smooth causal class containing both smoothed laws is non-point-identified for \(\ell_\star\), without any implication that the marked-capacity image is sharp in a larger nonmonotone class.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix one separated bump system from the strict-support proposition and use it under both signs.  Let \(H_{i,\delta}\) be the death bump centered at \(d_i^\star\), let \(J_{j,\delta}\) be the readmission bump centered at \(r_j^\star\), and retain point masses for the \(\infty\) categories.  Under either sign, the smoothed control within-arm law is
\[
 \mu_{0,\delta}^{\pm}
 =\sum_i\left(\sum_{h,j}q^\pm_{ihj}\right)
   (H_{i,\delta}\otimes\delta_\infty)
 =\sum_i\frac14(H_{i,\delta}\otimes\delta_\infty),                 \tag{44}
\]
so it is common to the two laws.  For the treated arm, the conditional kernel for \((D(1),R(1))\) depends only on \((h,j)\), even when the \(D(0)\) and \(D(1)\) bump draws are shared in an equal-death category.  Therefore
\[
 \mu_{1,\delta}^{\pm}
 =\sum_{h,j}\left(\sum_iq^\pm_{ihj}\right)
   (H_{h,\delta}\otimes J_{j,\delta})
 =\sum_{h,j}\mu_{1,hj}^\star
   (H_{h,\delta}\otimes J_{j,\delta}),                              \tag{45}
\]
which is also common.  These equalities prove equality of the complete smoothed within-arm laws, not merely equality of their death margins.

The strict-support proposition proves that the separated kernels preserve \(D(0)\leq D(1)\) and \(R(z)<D(z)\) whenever \(R(z)<\infty\), and that the finite-part within-arm densities are bounded and Lipschitz.  Use under both signs the same degenerate covariate, independent treatment with probability \(1/2\), and \(C=\tau=3\).  Consistency then gives, for every measurable observed-path set \(A\),
\[
 \Pr_{\pm,\delta}(O\in A)
 =\frac12\sum_{z=0}^1
   \int\mathbf 1\{\mathcal O(z,d,r,3)\in A\}\,
          d\mu_{z,\delta}^\star(d,r),                                \tag{46}
\]
where (44)--(45) show that the right side is independent of the sign.  Thus the two smooth laws are observationally equivalent.  The bump supports cross none of the death or readmission thresholds \(1,2,3\); the survivor denominators and the three numerators defining \(\ell_\star\) are consequently unchanged.  Since \(0<\eta\leq1/4\) keeps those coordinates in \(\mathcal H_\eta\), the two smooth laws retain the values \(-1/20\) and \(1/4\).

Any maintained smooth causal class containing both laws therefore has, at the common observable distribution (46), an identified set for \(\ell_\star\) containing two values separated by \(3/10\).  This proves non-point-identification.  It is only a two-witness containment argument and does not characterize the identified set after removal of terminal monotonicity.
added_lemmas.justification: This is the separate bounded-Lipschitz observational-equivalence certificate required before transferring the atomic nonidentification example to a maintained smooth class.
added_lemmas.gap: Smoothing two cross-world laws does not automatically preserve equality of their observed laws; equality of both smoothed within-arm margins must be checked after the shared-death construction.
added_lemmas.consumer: It supports smooth-class nonidentification while keeping the retained atomic transfer proposition logically narrow and leaving enlarged-class sharpness unclaimed.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: Suppose \(0<\eta\leq1/4\).  In the certified three-horizon construction \(\mathfrak E_3\), the full laws represented by \(q^-_{ihj}\) and \(q^+_{ihj}\) are distinct, satisfy \(D(0)\leq D(1)\), and induce the same observable distribution because both have within-arm laws \(\mu_0^\star\) and \(\mu_1^\star\) and the same treatment and censoring mechanisms.  Their projected couplings are \(f^-\) and \(f^+\), with \(\ell_\star(f^-)=-1/20\) and \(\ell_\star(f^+)=1/4\).  Hence every nonparametric causal model class containing both atomic laws is non-point-identified for \(\ell_\star\) at that common observed distribution.  This upward transfer is a nonidentification statement only; it does not assert that the marked-capacity image remains sharp after terminal monotonicity is removed.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The current claim omits the necessary premise that the three coordinates defining the signed surface functional lie in the target domain. The replacement adds the required condition \(0<\eta\leq1/4\). The distinct bounded-Lipschitz transfer is stated and proved separately rather than being inferred from the atomic pair.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed: For every Borel \(B\subseteq\mathcal E\), extend the boundary notation by \(s_x(\infty)=0\) and \(K_x(\infty,B)=0\).  Then \(A^U_x(r,t)=\inf_{u\in[t,\tau]\cup\{\infty\}}\{s_x(t)-s_x(u)+K_x(u,[0,r])\}\) and \(A^L_x(r,t)=\sup_{u\in[t,\tau]\cup\{\infty\}}\{s_x(u)-K_x(u,(r,\infty])\}\).
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The displayed optimization includes the isolated deadline \(u=\infty\), but the frozen construction defines only \(s_x(\infty)\) and leaves \(K_x(\infty,B)\) unspecified. The zero extension is forced by \(D(1)>\infty\) being the empty event and makes both boundary cuts well typed without changing any finite-deadline value.

proposed.statement: Suppose \(0<\eta\leq1/4\).  In the certified three-horizon construction \(\mathfrak E_3\), the full laws represented by \(q^-_{ihj}\) and \(q^+_{ihj}\) are distinct, satisfy \(D(0)\leq D(1)\), and induce the same observable distribution because both have within-arm laws \(\mu_0^\star\) and \(\mu_1^\star\) and the same treatment and censoring mechanisms.  Their projected couplings are \(f^-\) and \(f^+\), with \(\ell_\star(f^-)=-1/20\) and \(\ell_\star(f^+)=1/4\).  Hence every nonparametric causal model class containing both atomic laws is non-point-identified for \(\ell_\star\) at that common observed distribution.  This upward transfer is a nonidentification statement only; it does not assert that the marked-capacity image remains sharp after terminal monotonicity is removed.
proposed.justification: The two-law certificate transfers nonidentification to every larger causal class containing the certified atomic lifts without falsely transferring sharpness of the monotonicity-restricted capacity image.
proposed.gap: A strict support calculation inside the monotone class does not itself prove that the two atomic full laws induce the same observed distribution; the displayed observed-law mixture supplies that missing step.
proposed.consumer: Applied users who decline terminal monotonicity still obtain a certified atomic nonidentification conclusion, but not the monotonicity-restricted sharp capacity characterization.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The claim change adds the missing \(\eta\) free symbol and narrows the retained proposition to the atomic upward-transfer certificate; the smooth certificate is a separate proved proposition.

This proposition duplicates the retained atomic upward-transfer result. The retained proposition now contains the necessary target-domain premise, while the distinct bounded-Lipschitz observational-equivalence argument is preserved in a separate proved proposition.

prose_updates.tldr: Death truncates readmission, so the two-index TV-SACE and RM-SACE surfaces depend on an unidentified cross-world assignment of treated readmission times to control death times. Under arm-specific independent censoring through the full horizon and the additional maintained order \(D(0)\le D(1)\), the note characterizes the complete sharp monotonicity-restricted surface by a necessary-and-sufficient marked-capacity lift, proves common fixed-cohort extremizers and exact RM integration, and gives a certified three-horizon law whose joint cross-cohort support is strictly narrower than its coordinate rectangle. Quadratic chain flows, qualitative continuous-grid convergence, and deterministic-grid finite-sample outer containment make the population characterization computable. A joint marked-product-limit/IPCW functional limit, root-\(n\) grid-bias control, and simultaneous multiplier bands remain open.

project_justification.gap: Comment et al. define clinically meaningful TV-SACE and RM-SACE surfaces but leave their cross-world law to a parametric illness--death shared-frailty model and do not impose terminal monotonicity. Existing scalar or fixed-stratum bounds and generic transport formulations do not establish the complete readmission-specific capacity inequalities, a measurable four-time lift, or a smooth observational-equivalence witness for the changing always-survivor surface.
project_justification.niche: After separately auditing the additional restriction \(D(0)\le D(1)\), each always-survivor cohort becomes a nested marked-resource selection problem. This yields a sharp nonparametric class that is a subclass of the unrestricted causal model but generally incomparable with Comment et al.'s fitted shared-frailty family.
project_justification.fill: The note proves the monotonicity-restricted if-and-only-if capacity image, constructive full-law sharpness, common fixed-cohort extremizers, exact RM integration, a robust strict cross-cohort support example, quadratic computation, qualitative continuous approximation, and deterministic-grid finite-sample outer containment. The atomic three-horizon pair proves nonidentification in every larger class containing those atomic laws; a separate pair obtained with common separated bump kernels has identical smoothed within-arm laws and proves the corresponding nonidentification result in every maintained bounded-Lipschitz class containing that pair. Neither transfer claims enlarged-class capacity sharpness.

prose_updates.related_work: Comment, Mealli, Haneuse, and Zigler (2025) define the TV-SACE and RM-SACE estimands and estimate them with a Bayesian illness--death shared-frailty model. The present equality is instead a sharp nonparametric characterization after adding the audited restriction \(D(0)\le D(1)\); it is not an equality result for their unrestricted nonmonotone causal class, and their fitted shared-frailty family is generally incomparable with this monotonicity-restricted nonparametric class. Yang and Ding (2018) use detailed survival histories and copula sensitivity without monotonicity for scalar SACE bounds, which does not determine the nested compatible surface. Nevo and Gorfine (2022) study semi-competing-risk bounds under a single population stratification. Chen, Cui, and Yang (2024) transform fixed-time SACE programs and integrate scalar bounds but do not prove common changing-cohort surface extremizers. Strassen (1965) supplies the closed-relation coupling criterion; the readmission-marked cut reduction and full four-time lift are proved here. Russell (2021), Ober-Reynolds (2023), and Gao, Ge, and Qian (2024) motivate generic latent-law and transport programs, whereas the quadratic nested chain is specific to the maintained terminal order. The certified atomic and separated-bump pairs add direct observational-equivalence witnesses, including one inside the bounded-Lipschitz regime, but transfer only nonidentification to larger classes. Goldberg (2019) supplies standard IPCW recovery and concentration tools. Cho and Russell (2024), Bluhmki et al. (2019), Fang and Santos (2019), and Firpo, Galvao, and Parker (2023) inform the still-open simultaneous-inference route.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The marked-capacity image is proved sharp only over nonparametric full laws satisfying the maintained terminal-monotonicity restriction \(D(0)\le D(1)\), in addition to the stated exchangeability, event-order, overlap, and full-horizon censoring conditions. It is not asserted to equal the identified set in Comment et al.'s unrestricted nonmonotone class; without monotonicity, marked-capacity necessity and the denominator reduction can fail. When \(0<\eta\le1/4\), the two certified atomic lifts remain an observational-equivalence and nonidentification witness in any larger class containing them. Applying the same separated bump kernels to both lifts gives identical smoothed within-arm laws and a distinct observationally equivalent bounded-Lipschitz pair, so the same conclusion holds in every maintained smooth class containing that pair. Neither witness transfers capacity sharpness. The joint marked-process functional central limit theorem, estimated-censoring expansion, root-\(n\)-negligible grid bias, and simultaneous multiplier validity remain open.

statement_notes.gap: The strict-support calculation alone does not prove equality of the induced observed laws; the common within-arm mixture calculation supplies that step.
statement_notes.consumer: Users rejecting terminal monotonicity retain an atomic nonidentification certificate, with the required domain condition \(0<\eta\leq1/4\).

statement_notes.justification: The common-kernel construction separately certifies observational equivalence and distinct signed supports inside the bounded-Lipschitz regime.
statement_notes.gap: Atomic observational equivalence cannot be transferred to a smooth model by assertion; equality of both smoothed within-arm laws is proved after accounting for shared death draws.
